units.description: Name the parts of the body, say what hurts, and see a doctor.
units.tip: Pain works backwards from English: the body part is the subject, not you. "Masakit ang ulo ko" = my head hurts (literally "my head is painful"). Don't confuse it with "May sakit ako" — that one means "I'm sick".

units.title: Feelings & Opinions
units.description: Say how you feel, explain why, and give a simple opinion.
units.tip: Most Tagalog adjectives are ma- plus a root: saya (joy) → masaya, lungkot (sadness) → malungkot, init (heat) → mainit. A few feelings skip the ma- entirely — pagod, gutom, uhaw, galit, takot. Either way the feeling comes first: "Masaya ako", not "Ako ay masaya", which sounds stiff and bookish.

exercises.hint: The feeling goes first, the pronoun after it.

units.title: Colors & Clothing
units.description: Name colors, talk about clothes, and describe what people are wearing.
units.tip: A color before a noun needs a linker. After a vowel, add -ng: "pulang damit" (red clothes), "puting sapatos" (white shoes). After a consonant, use "na": "asul na sapatos" (blue shoes), "itim na pantalon" (black pants). As the predicate, drop the linker: "Pula ang damit." — The clothes are red.

kumusta.notes: From Spanish "¿cómo está?" — the everyday all-purpose greeting.

salamat.notes: "Salamat po" is more respectful; "maraming salamat" = thanks a lot.

hindi.notes: Negates verbs and adjectives too — "hindi masarap" = not delicious.

opo.notes: "po" makes speech polite; use with elders and strangers.

siya.notes: Tagalog pronouns are gender-neutral — siya means both he and she.

gusto.notes: Takes ng before the thing wanted: "Gusto ko ng kape."

ayaw.translation: to not like / to not want

araw_araw.notes: Reduplication — repeating a word — often means "every" or "each".

kuya.notes: Also used to politely address an older man.

ate.notes: Also used to politely address an older woman.

may.notes: "May kapatid ako." = I have a sibling.

wala.notes: Takes a linker: "Wala akong kapatid." = I have no sibling.

magkano.notes: Only for prices — "how many" of countable things is "ilan".

tindahan.notes: A small neighborhood shop; a "palengke" is a wet market.

bagyo.notes: The Philippines sees ~20 typhoons a year — this word matters.

saan.notes: Used with motion/action; "nasaan" asks the location of a thing.

diretso.notes: From Spanish "derecho". "Diretso lang" = just keep going straight.

jeepney.notes: A shared passenger jeep, the classic Philippine public transport.

ba.notes: "Malayo ba?" = Is it far? Turns a statement into a question.

mata.notes: One word for one eye or both — "Maganda ang mata mo." = Your eyes are beautiful.

tainga.notes: Usually shortened to "tenga" in casual speech.

paa.notes: The foot only — the leg is "binti".

likod.notes: Also "behind" — "sa likod ng bahay" = behind the house.

masakit.notes: The body part is the subject: "Masakit ang ulo ko." = My head hurts.

sakit.notes: "May sakit ako." = I am sick. Compare "masakit" = painful.

sipon.notes: The stuffy-nose kind of cold; cold weather is "malamig".

pagod.notes: No ma- on this one — just "Pagod ako."

gamot.notes: You drink medicine in Tagalog: "Uminom ka ng gamot." = Take your medicine.

doktor.notes: Used as a direct address too ("Salamat, doktor"); a woman doctor is often "doktora".

guro.notes: The standard word; "titser" (from English) is just as common in speech.

estudyante.notes: From Spanish "estudiante". "Mag-aaral" is the native word, used in writing.

drayber.notes: English "driver", spelled the Filipino way — jeepney and tricycle drivers included.

magsasaka.notes: From "saka" (to farm). Mag- plus a repeated syllable names many jobs.

tindera.notes: From "tinda" (goods for sale); a man is "tindero".

unibersidad.notes: "Kolehiyo" is college; "paaralan" covers school in general.

klase.notes: Also means kind or type: "Anong klase?" = What kind?

pagsusulit.notes: A written test or quiz; in casual speech many just say "exam" or "quiz".

matematika.notes: The formal subject name — day to day, people just say "math".

agham.notes: The native word; "science" is also very common in speech.

kasaysayan.notes: From "saysay" (account / meaning) — the telling of what happened.

ingles.notes: The language and the school subject; capitalized like other languages.

bolpen.notes: From English "ballpen" — the everyday word for a pen.

sahod.notes: "Sweldo" (from Spanish sueldo) is just as common in speech.

masaya.notes: ma- + saya (joy). "Masaya ako." = I am happy.

sabik.notes: "Sabik akong pumunta" = I am excited to go. In everyday speech many Filipinos just say the English "excited".

takot.notes: Takes sa for the thing feared: "Takot ako sa bagyo."

pakiramdam.notes: "Kumusta ang pakiramdam mo?" = How do you feel?

ayos_lang.notes: The everyday answer to "Kumusta ka?" when nothing much is wrong.

bakit.notes: Short pronouns hop in right after it: "Bakit ka malungkot?"

kasi.notes: The everyday spoken "because" — it starts the reason, never the sentence.

dahil.notes: The more formal twin of "kasi". "Dahil sa" + a noun = because of.

nakakatawa.notes: naka- + repeated syllable = "causes laughter". Formal spelling is nakatatawa.

nakakainis.notes: Same naka- pattern as nakakatawa — this one causes inis (irritation).

sa_tingin_ko.notes: Literally "in my view". Swap the pronoun to ask — "Sa tingin mo?"

medyo.notes: Goes before the adjective — "Medyo pagod ako."

sobra.notes: Takes -ng before an adjective: "Sobrang pagod ako." = I am so tired.

talaga.notes: On its own, "Talaga?" = Really? / Is that so?

banyo.notes: In public places Filipinos ask for the "CR" (comfort room) instead.

kwarto.notes: Also spelled "kuwarto"; the native word is "silid".

silya.notes: From Spanish "silla"; the native word "upuan" also works.

aparador.notes: Usually the tall cabinet where clothes are kept.

loob.notes: "Nasa loob ng bahay" = inside the house — "ng" links it to the place.

ibabaw.notes: "Nasa ibabaw ng mesa" = on top of the table.

naghuhugas.notes: Used for dishes and hands: "Naghuhugas ako ng plato."

tuloy_po_kayo.notes: Literally "go on through" — the standard welcome at a Filipino door.

kaarawan.notes: Built on "araw" (day). "Kaarawan ko ngayon." = It's my birthday today.

maligayang_kaarawan.notes: "maligaya" (happy) + the -ng linker — the set birthday greeting.

pista.notes: Every town and barangay honors its patron saint with a pista on the saint's day.

handa.notes: From "handa" (ready) — the food a host lays out for guests.

handaan.notes: The occasion itself; the "handa" is the food served at it.

kain_tayo.notes: Said to anyone within earshot when you start eating — an invitation, and a courtesy.

bagong_taon.notes: The greeting is "Manigong Bagong Taon!" — manigo means prosperous, not happy.

parol.notes: The star-shaped lantern hung up for Pasko.

simbang_gabi.translation: the nine dawn Masses before Christmas
simbang_gabi.notes: Held at dawn from December 16 to 24; finishing all nine is said to grant a wish.

binabati_kita.notes: From "bati" (greeting) — used for weddings, graduations and good news.

berde.notes: From Spanish "verde"; the native word "luntian" is more formal.

damit.notes: The general word for clothes; also a single garment.

kamiseta.notes: The everyday word for a shirt or T-shirt.

suot.notes: "Ano ang suot mo?" = What are you wearing?

nakasuot.notes: naka- means "in the state of". "Nakasuot siya ng pulang damit." = She is wearing a red dress.

kalabaw.notes: The national animal — the strong, patient work animal of the rice fields.

baboy.notes: Also the meat, pork — many rural families raise one in the backyard.

daga.notes: One word for both; do not confuse with "dagat" (sea).

alaga.notes: Anyone or anything you look after; takes a linker: "alagang aso" = pet dog.

tumatahol.notes: What a dog does; from "tahol" (a bark).

libangan.notes: From "libang" (to amuse oneself). "Ano ang libangan mo?" = What's your hobby?

hilig.notes: What you are into. "Ano ang hilig mo?" = What are you into?

maglaro.notes: The infinitive; "naglalaro" is the present (playing now).

basketbol.notes: The Philippines' most popular sport — a court stands in nearly every barangay.

kumanta.notes: In -um- verbs the infinitive and past look alike; "kumakanta" = singing now.

videoke.notes: Karaoke with a scoring machine — a fixture at nearly every Filipino party.

paborito.notes: From Spanish "favorito". Takes -ng before a noun — "paborito kong laro".
